etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stale, from Old French estale (“settled, clear”), but probably originally from Proto-Germanic *stāną (“to stand”): compare West Flemish stel in the same sense for ‘beer’ and ‘urine’.

definitions.definition: (alcoholic beverages, obsolete) Clear, free of dregs and lees; old and strong.

quote.citation: 1637, John Taylor, The Famovs Historie of the most part of Drinks, in use now in the Kingdomes of Great Brittaine and Ireland:
quote.text: The stronger Beere is divided into two parts (viz.) mild and stale; the first may ease a man of a drought, but the later is like water cast into a Smiths forge, and breeds more heartburning, and as rust eates into Iron, so overstale Beere gnawes auletholes in the entrales, or else my skill failes, and what I have written of it is to be held as a jest.

quote.citation: 1826, A Practical Man, The Vintner's, Brewer's, Spirit Merchant's, and Licensed Victualler's Guide, page 243:
quote.text: Particular care must be taken that the stale beer in which the isinglass is dissolved be perfectly clear and stale.

quote.citation: 1829, David Booth, The Art of Brewing, page 52:
quote.text: Is not that hard or stale beer mixed to give the porter the appearance of age at once, which formerly was allowed to be matured by time?

definitions.definition: No longer fresh, in reference to food, urine, straw, wounds, etc.

quote.citation: 1530, John Palsgrave, L'éclaircissement de la langue française‎[1], 325 2:
quote.text: Stale as breed or drinke is, rassis. Stale as meate is that begynneth to savoure, viel.

quote.citation: c. 1550, Wyll of Deuill, C 2 b:
quote.text: New freshe blood to ouersprinkle their stale mete that it may seme...newly kylled.

quote.citation: 2012, Stephen Woodworth, In Golden Blood: Number 3 in series:
quote.text: To her surprise, Abe did not come to collect her for the usual morning inhabitation session with Azure. She did not see him until almost noon, when he personally delivered lunch to her tent. Another stale roll and cup of water sat on the tray he carried. Abe hung his head, as abashed as Honorato had been. “This is all I could sneak in for now. I'll try to get more later.”

definitions.definition: No longer fresh, new, or interesting, in reference to ideas and immaterial things; clichéd, hackneyed, dated.

quote.citation: 1562, Proverbs & Epigrams, J. Heywood, published 1867, section 95:
quote.text: Better is...be it new or stale, A harmelesse lie, than a harmefull true tale.

quote.citation: 1579, in G. Harvey, letter book, 60:
quote.text: Doist thou smyle to reade this stale and beggarlye stuffe.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], line 133:

quote.citation: 1822 March, Charles Lamb, London Magazine, 284 1:
quote.text: A two-days-old newspaper. You resent the stale thing as an affront.

quote.citation: 2002, Mark Lawson, And They Rose Up: Days of Retribution:
quote.text: Rick would comment on the fact that he'd never had such bad coffee, not even the mud at his precinct. Mark would tell him to quit with the stale joke, already

definitions.definition: (obsolete) No longer nubile or suitable for marriage, in reference to people; past one's prime.

quote.citation: c. 1580, J. Jeffere, Bugbears, I ii 108:
quote.text: Rosimunda...hathe an vncle a stale batcheler.

quote.citation: 1742, T. Short, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 42 226:
quote.text: In barren Women, and stale Maids, Tapping should be very cautiously undertaken.

definitions.definition: (in general) Not new or recent; having been in place or in effect for some time.

quote.citation: 2014, David L. Hough, Street Strategies for Motorcyclists:
quote.text: In most states, you can be ticketed for failing to clear the intersection, even if you are hemmed in by traffic. One good clue to a stale green light is the pedestrian signal.

definitions.definition: (agriculture, obsolete) Fallow, in reference to land.

quote.citation: 1764, Museum Rusticum, II 306:
quote.text: Lime would do very little or no good on stale ploughed lands.

definitions.definition: (law) Unreasonably long in coming, in reference to claims and actions.

quote.citation: 1769, William Blackstone, Common Laws of England, IV xv 211:
quote.text: The jury will rarely give credit to a stale complaint.

definitions.definition: Worn out, particularly due to age or over-exertion, in reference to athletes and animals in competition.

quote.citation: 1856, “Stonehenge”, in Manual of British Rural Sports, II i vi §7 335:
quote.text: By this means the [horse's] legs are not made more stale than necessary.
Dame Agnes will probably be stale after her exertions in the Derby.

definitions.definition: (finance) Out of date, unpaid for an unreasonable amount of time, particularly in reference to checks.

quote.citation: 1901, Business Terms & Phrases, second edition, 199:
quote.text: Stale cheque,...a cheque which has remained unpaid for some considerable time.

definitions.definition: (computing) Of data: out of date; not synchronized with the newest copy.
(colloquial) Something stale; a loaf of bread or the like that is no longer fresh.

quote.text: Frayed-looking sweet-cakes...bought as ‘stales’ from the baker.

definitions.definition: (of alcohol, obsolete, transitive) To make stale; to age in order to clear and strengthen (a drink, especially beer).

quote.citation: c. 1440, Promp. Parv., 472 1:
quote.text: Stalyn, or make stale drynke, defeco.

quote.citation: 1826, Art of Brewing, second edition, 106:
quote.text: A stock of old porter should be kept, sufficient for staling the consumption of twelve months.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make stale; to cause to go out of fashion or currency; to diminish the novelty or interest of, particularly by excessive exposure or consumption.

quote.citation: 1601, Ben Jonson, Fountaine of Self-love, section 36:
quote.text: Ile goe tell all the Argument of his Play aforehand, and so stale his Inuention to the Auditory before it come foorth.

quote.citation: 1598, Beniamin Ionson [i.e., Ben Jonson], “Euery Man in His Humour. A Comœdie. […]”, in The Workes of Beniamin Ionson (First Folio), London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby, published 1616, →OCLC, Act I, scene iv:
quote.text: Not content To stale himselfe in all societies, He makes my house as common as a Mart.

quote.text: Age cannot wither her, nor custome stale Her infinite variety.

quote.citation: 1863, W. W. Story, Roba di Roma, I i 7:
quote.text: Pictures and statues have been staled by copy and description.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become stale; to grow odious from excessive exposure or consumption.

quote.citation: 1717, E. Erskine, Serm. in Wks., 50 1:
quote.text: They have got so much of Christ as to be staled of his company.

quote.citation: 1893, “Q”, in Delectable Duchy, section 325:

definitions.definition: (alcoholic beverages, intransitive) To become stale; to grow unpleasant from age.

quote.citation: 1742, W. Ellis, London & Country Brewer, 4th edition, I 64:
quote.text: The Drink from that Time flattens and stales.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stale, from Old English stalu, from Proto-Germanic *stal-; compare English stell from this root. The development was paralleled by the ablaut which became English steal, from Middle English stele, from Old English stela, from Proto-Germanic *stel-. Both are from the same Proto-Indo-European root *stel-, *stol- (“to place, establish”), whence also Ancient Greek στελεός (steleós, “handle”). See also English stele.

definitions.definition: A long, thin handle (of rakes, axes, etc.)

quote.citation: 1742, W. Ellis, London & Country Brewer, 4th edition, I 61:
quote.text: In Case your Cask is a Butt,...have ready boiling...Water, which put in, and, with a long Stale and a little Birch fastened to its End, scrub the Bottom.

quote.citation: 1890 February 4, Manchester Guardian, 12 3:
quote.text: You came to me with the axe head in one hand and the stale in the other.

definitions.definition: (dialectal) One of the posts or uprights of a ladder.

quote.citation: 1887, W. D. Parish et al., Kentish Dial.:
quote.text: Stales, the staves, or risings of a ladder, or the staves of a rack in a stable.

quote.text: Fruit ladders should be provided beforehand. They differ from the ordinary ladder by having the bottom rungs a little longer and the top of the side stales meeting together so is to rest in the fork of a limb.

quote.citation: 1971, Research Paper - Issues 141-155, page 7:
quote.text: The zigzag determines the order of the currents from [1] which occur on the stales of the ladder and their relation with the currents from [0] which occur on the rungs and ringles between them.

definitions.definition: One of the rungs on a ladder.

quote.text: To begin then: not long before this paragraph was written, P fell into doze, and dreamt, he saw Jacob's ladder with one foot standing on the earth, the other reaching up into heaven. quote.citation: 1834, Joseph Adshead, A Circumstantial Narrative of the Wreck of the Rothsay, page 236:
quote.text: Mr. Marsden managed, by dint of swimming, to come in contact with the form, to which hemself and friend had previously fixed the cord and thrown overboard; but this, from its shape, would have proved, in all probability, but a doubtful means of escape, had he not, after a time, fallen in with a small ladder, which he affixed with the cord to the form, placing his leg between the stales, and resting his body, sometimes at full length, when the breakers had fallen on the form.

quote.text: The rental of the lands remained at these figures for many years, and the following extracts are examples of the payments made:— A.D. 1686, Utt, pd Thomas Rassel for a load of lime delivered to Smalhith Chappell 01₤ 11s. 0d. Itt . for a quire of paper 00₤ 00s. 06d. Itt . for a ladder for the use of the Chappel 33 stales long , at 2d ye stale 00₤ 05s. 6d.

quote.citation: 1998, Barney Edward Daley, Tobacco Parish: A Collection of South Windsor's Memories:
quote.text: Ash was used for stales (ladder rungs).

quote.citation: 2014, Matthew Engel, Engel's England: Thirty-nine counties, one capital and one man:
quote.text: As a young man Mike Austen, a retired farmer now working as a guide at Brogdale, used to climb up a ladder with sixty 'stales', or rungs – eight inches between each of them – to pick the cherries in his father's orchard with a basket tied to either his waist or the ladder.

definitions.definition: (botany, obsolete) The stem of a plant.
The shaft of an arrow, spear, etc.

quote.citation: 1492, Archæol. Cant., XVI 304:
quote.text: For stalyng of the ladders of the Churche xx d.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stale, from Old French estal (“place, something placed”) (compare French étal), from Frankish stal, from Proto-Germanic *stallaz, earlier *staþlaz. Related to stall and stand.

definitions.definition: (military, obsolete) A fixed position, particularly a soldier's in a battle-line.

quote.citation: 1550, Edward Halle, The Vnion of the Two Noble and Illustre Famelies of Lancastre and Yorke:
quote.text: Wherefore they had a great avauntage, but in coclusion thie french menne were slayne, and their horses taken, and so the lyght horsement came wyth their catail, nere to the embushment, and the frenchimen folowed, that seyng the englyshmen that kept the stale, came in al hast & rescued their light horsemen, and draue the frenchemen backe, & then made returne to their beastes

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Noun from Middle English stale, from Anglo-Norman estal (“urine”), from Middle Dutch stal (“urine”). Cognate with Middle Low German stal (“horse urine; bowel movement”). Verb from Middle English stalen, from Old French estaler (“urinate”), related to Middle High German stallen (“to piss”).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stale (“bird used as a decoy”), probably from uncommon Anglo-Norman estale (“pigeon used to lure hawks”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic, probably *standaną (“to stand”).
